results.title: Corrective Action Plans (CAPs) for Enrollment Progress | National Institute on Aging
results.content: The NIA has instituted the NIA Clinical Research Enrollment Policy (NOT-AG-24-081) to address NIA clinical trials with participant enrollment progress indicating that the clinical trial is delayed and may not be completed on time. This policy applies to all NIA grants, contracts, and cooperative agreements that support human subjects research that are required to electronically submit participant enrollment data into the secure NIA Clinical Research Operations & Management System (CROMS) on a monthly basis, per NIA Update to Policy and Procedures for the Reporting of Human Subjects Enrollment Data for NIA Clinical Research Trials/Studies (NOT-AG-23-017), and is effective immediately. NIA requires the submission of a Corrective Action Plan (CAP) for clinical trials whose timeline milestones and participant enrollment indicate that the clinical trial is delayed, and the rate of enrollment is less than 60% of its expected benchmark. This policy aims to ensure compliance with timely clinical trial enrollment progress which improves transparency and accountability and helps achieve recruitment and retention goals for studies focused on improving the health and well-being of older Americans.

results.title: Clinical Trial Enrollment Caps: What They Are And When To Use Them
results.content: Clinical Trial Enrollment Caps: What They Are And When To Use Them | Pharmaceutical Outsourcing - The Journal of Pharmaceutical & Biopharmaceutical Contract Services. However, the second question “Should I have an enrollment cap for sites on my study?” is not as easy to answer. Positively speaking, site enrollment caps mitigate the risk of confounding treatment and side effects, which is critical to ensuring that regulators accept the study as evidence of a drug’s efficacy. These caps also require more sites to participate in study enrollment, which can improve the chances of your study having a diverse pool of subjects. Logistically speaking, some sites will likely under-enroll, and placing a cap on high-enrolling sites can result in a longer trial (particularly if the enrollment caps are low). Compared to a study with no cap, it also means that your trial will ultimately require more sites than otherwise planned. Lastly, when implementing an enrollment cap, it is important to manage your relationships with the study sites. Enrollment caps can cause frustration among high-enrolling sites if they have more subjects to offer to the trial. **Design:** 400 subjects per study were competitively enrolled in a randomized, active-controlled trial taking place at approximately 40 sites. **Implementation:** Given that each trial site/surgical center tended to focus on a subset of surgeries, an enrollment cap of 25 subjects per site was set to ensure that no site dominated the trial enrollment, allowing for a more diverse group of surgery indications to be represented in the study. However, given site start-up delays, some under-enrolling sites and enrollment caps being enforced, the study ended up enrolling for 3x of the projected enrollment period. a. Both studies achieved a diverse mix of sites and surgery types via the use of enrollment caps to broadly represent how the drug could potentially be utilized. In conclusion, enrollment caps are a tool that can be used during a clinical trial to minimize the risk of confounding a side effect with that of the treatment under investigation. When planning your next clinical trial, consulting with regulatory and statistical experts is advisable, as they can help navigate these tricky waters and determine if site enrollment caps make sense for your specific program’s development.

results.content: ## GENE ONLINE|News & Opinion Blog ### Clinical Trial Enrollment Strategies Focus on Risk Mitigation and Diversity Compliance ##### Share To Clinical trial teams recognize risk mitigation as a fundamental component of trial success, and this principle extends to enrollment strategies. Effective recruitment and enrollment plans require careful consideration of potential risks that could impact the progress and outcomes of clinical studies. Key factors to address in enrollment planning include identifying barriers to participant recruitment, ensuring diversity among study participants, and maintaining compliance with regulatory requirements. Recruitment challenges often arise from insufficient outreach or lack of awareness among eligible participants. Diversity considerations are critical for ensuring that trial results are representative across different demographics, while adherence to regulations safeguards the integrity of the study. These elements collectively play a vital role in minimizing risks associated with delays or data inconsistencies during clinical trials.
